Adult Cardiac Arrest:
[b]Emergency & Critical Care[/b]
Guideline basis: 2025 American Heart Association (AHA) Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care.

Suspect cardiac arrest when an adult patient is:
• Unresponsive.
• Not breathing normally (apnea or agonal gasping).
• Without a definite central pulse.

[b]Pulse check:[/b] Check carotid or femoral pulse for no more than 10 seconds.

[b]Immediate action:[/b]
• Activate the resuscitation/code team.
• Start high-quality CPR immediately.
• Attach monitor/defibrillator as soon as available.
• Do not delay CPR for ECG, investigations, or IV access.

[b]Chest compressions:[/b]
• Rate: 100–120 compressions/min.
• Depth: At least 5 cm (2 inches), avoiding excessive depth.
• Allow complete chest recoil.
• Minimize interruptions; pauses should be less than 10 seconds.
• Change compressor approximately every 2 minutes or sooner if fatigued.
• Keep the patient supine on a firm surface.

[b]Compression-to-ventilation ratio:[/b]
• Without advanced airway: 30 compressions : 2 breaths.
• With advanced airway: Continuous compressions with 1 breath every 6 seconds (10 breaths/min).

[b]Ventilation:[/b]
• Use bag-mask ventilation with 100% oxygen.
• Deliver each breath over approximately 1 second, producing visible chest rise.
• Avoid excessive ventilation.

[b]Monitoring:[/b]
• Use waveform capnography when an advanced airway is placed.
• Low ETCO₂ prompts reassessment of CPR quality.
• Sudden sustained increase in ETCO₂ may indicate ROSC.

After starting CPR and attaching the monitor:

[b]Shockable rhythms:[/b]
• Ventricular fibrillation (VF).
• Pulseless ventricular tachycardia (pVT).

[b]Non-shockable rhythms:[/b]
• Asystole.
• Pulseless electrical activity (PEA).

[b]Important:[/b] Neither Asystole nor PEA is treated with defibrillation.

[b]Immediate management:[/b]
1. Deliver an unsynchronized defibrillation shock.
2. Immediately resume CPR for 2 minutes without checking the pulse.
3. Obtain IV access (or IO if IV is delayed).
4. Reassess rhythm after 2 minutes.
5. If still VF/pVT, deliver another shock and resume CPR.
6. Administer epinephrine after initial defibrillation attempts have failed, then repeat every 3–5 minutes.
7. If VF/pVT persists, administer amiodarone or lidocaine.
8. Continue cycles of CPR, shocks, medications, and treat reversible causes.

[b]Defibrillation Energy:[/b]
• Biphasic: 120–200 J (or max available).
• Monophasic: 360 J.

[b]1. Epinephrine (Adrenaline)[/b]
• Dose: 1 mg IV/IO every 3–5 minutes.
• Timing: Give after initial defibrillation attempts have failed.
• Warning: Do not confuse 1 mg/10 mL (0.1 mg/mL) with 1 mg/mL ampoules. Confirm concentration before administration.

[b]2. Amiodarone[/b]
• Indication: Refractory VF/pulseless VT.
• First dose: 300 mg IV/IO bolus.
• Second dose: 150 mg IV/IO if VF/pVT persists.

[b]3. Lidocaine (Alternative to amiodarone)[/b]
• First dose: 1–1.5 mg/kg IV/IO.
• Second dose: 0.5–0.75 mg/kg IV/IO.
• Do not routinely administer both amiodarone and lidocaine together.
• For a 70 kg adult: Initial 70–105 mg, Second dose 35–52.5 mg.

[b]Immediate management:[/b]
• Start or continue high-quality CPR immediately.
• Confirm rhythm and check monitor connections.
• Obtain IV/IO access.
• Administer epinephrine (1 mg IV/IO) as soon as possible, repeat every 3–5 minutes.
• Perform CPR cycles of 2 minutes and reassess rhythm.
• If the rhythm becomes VF/pVT, switch immediately to the shockable pathway.

[b]Important warnings:[/b]
• Do NOT defibrillate asystole.
• Do NOT defibrillate PEA.
• Do NOT interrupt CPR for prolonged rhythm checks.

[b]Hs:[/b]
• Hypovolemia (Control bleeding, give fluids/blood).
• Hypoxia (Secure airway, give oxygen).
• Hydrogen ion - Acidosis (Optimize CPR; sodium bicarbonate NOT routinely recommended).
• Hypo/Hyperkalemia (Check electrolytes, treat specific abnormalities).
• Hypothermia (Begin rewarming).

[b]Ts:[/b]
• Tension pneumothorax (Immediate decompression).
• Cardiac tamponade (Urgent pericardial drainage).
• Toxins (Identify agent, give specific antidotes).
• Pulmonary thrombosis (Consider thrombolysis).
• Coronary thrombosis (Urgent coronary reperfusion after ROSC).

[b]Airway:[/b]
• Start with bag-mask ventilation and airway adjuncts.
• Consider endotracheal intubation or supraglottic airway by an experienced operator.
• Avoid prolonged interruption of compressions during placement.
• Confirm with continuous waveform capnography.
• After advanced airway: 1 breath every 6 seconds (10 breaths/min). Avoid hyperventilation.

[b]IV / IO Access:[/b]
• Establish IV access without interrupting CPR. If IV fails rapidly, use IO.
• Do not delay defibrillation or epinephrine for IV access.

The following are [b]NOT[/b] routinely indicated during cardiac arrest unless for specific circumstances:
• [b]Sodium bicarbonate:[/b] Only for specific indications (e.g., hyperkalemia, TCA toxicity).
• [b]Calcium:[/b] Only for hyperkalemia, hypocalcemia, or CCB toxicity.
• [b]Magnesium:[/b] Consider only for torsades de pointes or hypomagnesemia.
• [b]Vasopressin:[/b] Not recommended as a routine substitute for epinephrine.
• [b]High-dose epinephrine:[/b] Not recommended.

[b]Signs suggesting ROSC:[/b]
• Palpable central pulse.
• Sudden sustained increase in ETCO₂.
• Spontaneous breathing or purposeful movement.
• Measurable blood pressure.

[b]Immediate actions after ROSC:[/b]
• Confirm pulse and obtain BP.
• Maintain oxygenation (Target SpO₂: 90–98%).
• Avoid hypotension; maintain MAP at least 65 mmHg.
• Obtain 12-lead ECG; assess for coronary occlusion.
• Check blood gas, electrolytes, glucose, lactate.
• Consider targeted temperature control if unresponsive.

Decisions must follow local institutional protocols and applicable termination-of-resuscitation rules.

• Consider the initial rhythm, witnessed status, bystander CPR, response to treatment, reversible causes, and overall clinical context.
• Do not terminate solely because a specific duration of CPR has elapsed or because ETCO₂ is low.
• Consider special circumstances: hypothermia, poisoning, pregnancy, and pulmonary embolism.
• Document the clinical findings, interventions, response, and decision-making.

• Early high-quality CPR and rapid defibrillation are the most important interventions for VF/pVT.
• Do not delay the first shock in a shockable rhythm.
• Resume CPR immediately after every shock.
• Epinephrine is given as soon as possible in PEA/asystole.
• Rhythm and pulse checks should not interrupt CPR for more than 10 seconds.
• Always search for and treat reversible causes (Hs and Ts).
• Assign clear team roles: team leader, compressor, airway operator, defibrillator operator, medication nurse, and recorder.

• American Heart Association. 2025 Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care. Part 9: Adult Advanced Life Support.
• American Heart Association. 2025 Adult Cardiac Arrest Algorithm.

[b]Clinical note:[/b] This reference is intended for trained healthcare professionals. Follow current local resuscitation protocols and institutional medication preparation policies.

Nephritic Syndrome: Nephritic syndrome is a clinical presentation of glomerular inflammation characterized by hematuria, dysmorphic red blood cells or red-cell casts, reduced kidney function in some patients, hypertension, and variable proteinuria. It may progress rapidly to acute kidney injury and requires prompt evaluation.

- Dark, tea-colored, or cola-colored urine.
- Microscopic or visible hematuria.
- Periorbital or peripheral edema.
- Hypertension, sometimes severe.
- Oliguria or reduced urine output.
- Elevated serum creatinine.
- Proteinuria, usually less prominent than in classic nephrotic syndrome, although overlap occurs.

- IgA nephropathy.
- Post-infectious glomerulonephritis.
- Lupus nephritis.
- ANCA-associated vasculitis.
- Anti-glomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM) disease.
- Other immune-complex or infection-associated glomerular diseases.

- Assess ABCs, blood pressure, oxygen saturation, and volume status.
- Check urine output and obtain urgent renal function and electrolyte measurements.
- Look for hypertensive emergency, pulmonary edema, severe hyperkalemia, or uremic complications.
- Obtain urinalysis and urine microscopy.
- Evaluate for rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, particularly if creatinine is rising quickly.
- Consult nephrology urgently when renal function deteriorates or a systemic vasculitic process is suspected.
- Do not delay specialist-directed treatment in a life-threatening pulmonary-renal syndrome.

[b]Initial investigations:[/b]
- Urinalysis and urine microscopy for dysmorphic RBCs and RBC casts.
- Urine protein-to-creatinine ratio or albumin-to-creatinine ratio.
- Serum creatinine, urea, eGFR, electrolytes, and bicarbonate.
- CBC, serum albumin, and inflammatory markers as indicated.
- Blood pressure monitoring and strict fluid balance.
- Renal ultrasound when obstruction or abnormal renal anatomy needs exclusion.

[b]Immunological & infectious investigations:[/b]
- C3 and C4 complement levels.
- ANA and anti-dsDNA when lupus is suspected.
- ANCA testing when vasculitis is suspected.
- Anti-GBM antibodies.
- ASO and anti-DNase B when recent streptococcal infection is suspected.
- Hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HIV, blood cultures, and other infection studies.

[b]Renal biopsy:[/b]
- Often required when the cause is unclear, renal function is deteriorating, or immunosuppressive treatment is being considered.

[b]Dose:[/b] There is no universal fluid dose for nephritic syndrome. Individualize fluid and sodium intake according to volume status, urine output, renal function, and serum sodium.

[b]Administration and monitoring:[/b]
- Restrict dietary sodium when fluid retention or hypertension is present.
- Monitor daily weight, intake/output, blood pressure, electrolytes, and creatinine.
- If pulmonary edema or severe volume overload develops, provide urgent monitored treatment.

[b]WARNING:[/b]
- Do not automatically give large volumes of IV fluid to a patient with oliguria, hypertension, or pulmonary edema.
- Fluid restriction must be individualized, particularly if there is concurrent hypovolemia.

[b]Dose:[/b] Furosemide 20–40 mg IV may be used initially in adults with clinically significant fluid overload, with adjustment according to renal function and response.

[b]Administration and monitoring:[/b]
- Monitor urine output, blood pressure, electrolytes, renal function, and respiratory status.
- Escalate treatment or use additional strategies under specialist guidance if pulmonary edema is not responding.

[b]WARNING:[/b]
- Diuretics treat fluid overload but do not treat the underlying glomerular inflammation.
- Avoid excessive diuresis in patients with intravascular depletion.

[b]Management:[/b]
- Treat severe hypertension according to the acute hypertension protocol, particularly if there is encephalopathy, myocardial ischemia, acute kidney injury, or pulmonary edema.
- In a hypertensive emergency, use a monitored IV agent appropriate to the affected organ system and lower blood pressure in a controlled manner.

[b]WARNING:[/b]
- Avoid rapid, uncontrolled blood pressure reduction.
- ACE inhibitors and ARBs may be useful for persistent hypertension and proteinuria in selected stable patients, but may be unsuitable during acute kidney injury or hyperkalemia.

- Treat severe hyperkalemia immediately using the emergency hyperkalemia protocol.
- Review and stop contributing medications where appropriate.
- Avoid nephrotoxins, including NSAIDs, when possible.
- Adjust drug doses to current renal function.
- Obtain urgent nephrology input for rapidly progressive renal dysfunction.

[b]Indications for urgent dialysis assessment:[/b]
- Refractory hyperkalemia.
- Severe metabolic acidosis not responding to medical treatment.
- Pulmonary edema or fluid overload resistant to treatment.
- Uremic complications, such as encephalopathy or pericarditis.

- [b]Post-infectious glomerulonephritis:[/b] Supportive care, fluid and blood pressure management.
- [b]IgA nephropathy:[/b] Supportive kidney-protective treatment; immunomodulatory therapy only for selected patients under nephrology guidance.
- [b]Lupus nephritis:[/b] Biopsy-guided immunosuppressive therapy based on disease class and severity.
- [b]ANCA-associated vasculitis:[/b] Urgent specialist-directed induction therapy, often involving glucocorticoids plus rituximab or cyclophosphamide.
- [b]Anti-GBM disease:[/b] Urgent specialist-directed therapy, commonly involving plasma exchange and immunosuppression.

[b]WARNING:[/b] Do not start routine high-dose corticosteroids in every patient with nephritic syndrome. Immunosuppression can worsen untreated infection and must be guided by the suspected diagnosis.

- Frequent blood pressure assessment.
- Strict urine output and fluid balance.
- Serial creatinine, potassium, bicarbonate, and other electrolytes.
- Urinalysis and proteinuria monitoring.
- Assessment for pulmonary edema, uremic symptoms, and systemic vasculitic manifestations.
- Follow-up complement and disease-specific markers when relevant.

[b]Urgent admission and nephrology consultation are indicated for:[/b]
- Rapidly rising creatinine or suspected rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis.
- Oliguria or anuria.
- Severe hypertension or hypertensive emergency.
- Pulmonary edema.
- Significant hyperkalemia or metabolic acidosis.
- Suspected ANCA-associated vasculitis or anti-GBM disease, especially with hemoptysis or hypoxemia.

[b]Stable patients[/b] still require timely nephrology evaluation to establish the cause and assess the need for kidney biopsy.

- Nephritic syndrome is characterized by glomerular hematuria and inflammation, often with hypertension and impaired renal function.
- RBC casts strongly support a glomerular source of bleeding.
- Hemoptysis plus acute kidney injury should raise concern for a pulmonary-renal syndrome.
- Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis is a time-critical diagnosis because early treatment may preserve kidney function.
- Nephritic and nephrotic features can coexist in the same patient.

[b]References:[/b]
KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Glomerular Diseases, 2021.
KDIGO Guidance on ANCA-associated vasculitis and lupus nephritis.

[b]Disclaimer:[/b] This material is a clinical reference aid, not a substitute for nephrology consultation, kidney biopsy when indicated, or current local treatment protocols.
Nephrotic Syndrome:
A clinical disorder caused by increased glomerular permeability to plasma proteins, resulting in significant urinary protein loss.

[b]Diagnostic features:[/b]
• Heavy proteinuria: ≥3.5 g/24 hours in adults.
• Hypoalbuminemia: commonly serum albumin <3.0 g/dL.
• Peripheral edema.
• Hyperlipidemia and lipiduria.

[b]Spot urine alternative:[/b]
• Urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPCR) ≥3–3.5 g/g is generally consistent with nephrotic-range proteinuria.
• A 24-hour urine collection may be used when more precise quantification is needed.

[b]Typical presentation:[/b]
• Bilateral pitting edema, initially involving the lower limbs.
• Periorbital edema, particularly in the morning.
• Progressive weight gain due to fluid retention.
• Frothy or foamy urine.
• Ascites, pleural effusion (in severe cases).
• Fatigue and reduced exercise tolerance.

[b]Clinical examination:[/b]
• Blood pressure may be normal or elevated.
• Assess volume status carefully.
• Look for signs of underlying systemic disease (infection, VTE).

[b]Important findings:[/b] Generalized edema (anasarca), severe hypoalbuminemia, reduced urine output, features of DVT or PE.

Glomerular filtration barrier injury causes excessive urinary albumin and protein loss.

This leads to:
• Hypoalbuminemia and reduced plasma oncotic pressure.
• Fluid movement into the interstitial space and edema.
• Activation of sodium-retaining mechanisms.
• Increased hepatic lipoprotein synthesis and reduced lipid clearance (hyperlipidemia).
• Urinary loss of immunoglobulins and anticoagulant proteins, increasing infection and thrombosis risk.

[b]1. Primary Glomerular Diseases:[/b]
• Minimal Change Disease (MCD).
• Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS).
• Membranous Nephropathy.
• Other less common glomerular disorders.

[b]2. Secondary Causes:[/b]
• [b]Diabetes mellitus:[/b] Diabetic kidney disease is a major cause.
• [b]Systemic diseases:[/b] SLE, Amyloidosis, Multiple myeloma, Vasculitis.
• [b]Infections:[/b] Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, HIV.
• [b]Medications:[/b] NSAIDs, Interferons, Lithium.
• [b]Malignancy:[/b] Solid tumors and hematological malignancies (especially in membranous nephropathy).

[b]Immediate assessment:[/b]
• Assess ABCs if acutely unwell.
• Measure BP, HR, RR, Temp, SpO₂.
• Assess edema severity, distribution, and body weight.
• Assess urine output and intravascular volume status.
• Look for infection, thrombosis, or AKI.

[b]Red flags:[/b]
• Sudden dyspnea or pleuritic chest pain → Pulmonary embolism.
• Unilateral painful leg swelling → DVT.
• Fever or abdominal pain → Infection (e.g., spontaneous bacterial peritonitis).
• Oliguria or rapidly increasing creatinine → AKI.
• Severe hypertension or neurological symptoms → Hypertensive emergency.

[b]1. Urine:[/b]
• Urinalysis (heavy proteinuria, lipiduria, microscopic hematuria).
• Quantification (UPCR, UACR, 24-hour urine protein).
• Urine microscopy (oval fat bodies, fatty casts).

[b]2. Blood:[/b]
• Serum albumin, total protein.
• Serum creatinine, urea, eGFR, electrolytes.
• Lipid profile, CBC, LFTs.
• Blood glucose and HbA1c.

[b]3. Secondary Causes (as indicated):[/b]
• ANA, anti-dsDNA (Lupus).
• C3, C4.
• Hepatitis B/C, HIV.
• Serum/urine protein electrophoresis, free light chains (Myeloma).
• Anti-PLA2R antibodies (Membranous).

[b]4. Imaging:[/b] Renal ultrasound (kidney size, structure, exclude obstruction).

[b]Indications:[/b]
• Adults with unexplained new-onset nephrotic syndrome.
• Suspected FSGS, membranous nephropathy, or secondary glomerular disease.
• Atypical clinical features.
• Rapid deterioration in renal function.
• Persistent proteinuria despite management.

[b]May NOT be immediately required:[/b]
• Typical diabetic kidney disease with convincing history.
• Selected patients where biopsy would not change management.

[b]Important:[/b] Coordinate with nephrology. Assess BP, platelets, coagulation, and bleeding risk before biopsy.

[b]Dietary sodium restriction:[/b] ~2 g/day (about 5 g salt).
[b]Fluid restriction:[/b] Not routinely required. Consider in severe edema, hyponatremia, or fluid overload.

[b]Loop diuretics (First-line):[/b]
• Furosemide: 20–40 mg PO once/twice daily. IV: 20–40 mg IV (adjust per response).
• Higher doses may be needed in severe edema or reduced kidney function.

[b]Monitoring:[/b] BP, urine output, daily weight, fluid balance, electrolytes (Na, K, Mg), renal function.

[b]Warning:[/b] Patients may have reduced effective circulating volume despite generalized edema. Excessive diuresis can cause hypotension, AKI, and electrolyte disturbances.

[b]Resistant edema:[/b] Consider thiazide + loop combination, or IV albumin followed by IV furosemide in selected severe cases.

[b]ACE inhibitors:[/b] Enalapril, Ramipril, Lisinopril.
[b]ARBs:[/b] Losartan, Valsartan.

[b]Approach:[/b]
• Start at a low dose and titrate according to BP, kidney function, and potassium.
• Monitor creatinine and potassium after initiation and dose escalation.
• Do NOT combine ACE inhibitors and ARBs routinely.

[b]Warnings:[/b]
• Avoid during pregnancy.
• Use caution in hypotension, hyperkalemia, or AKI.
• Reassess if serum creatinine rises significantly.

[b]Lipid Management:[/b]
• Obtain lipid profile.
• Address CV risk factors.
• Consider statins per LDL, CV risk, age, and CKD status.
• Hyperlipidemia may improve when nephrotic syndrome is controlled.

[b]Underlying Cause:[/b]
• [b]MCD:[/b] Glucocorticoids are commonly used as initial therapy in adults (after evaluation).
• [b]FSGS:[/b] Distinguish primary vs secondary/genetic. Immunosuppression reserved for selected primary cases.
• [b]Membranous:[/b] Check anti-PLA2R. Risk-stratify. Immunosuppression for high-risk/progressive disease.
• [b]Diabetic Kidney Disease:[/b] Optimize glycemic control, BP, ACEi/ARB, consider SGLT2i.
• [b]Lupus Nephritis:[/b] Coordinate with nephrology/rheumatology.

[b]Warning:[/b] Do NOT start high-dose steroids/immunosuppression empirically without diagnostic assessment.

[b]Thromboembolism Risk:[/b]
• Increased risk (especially membranous nephropathy and severe hypoalbuminemia).
• Assess for DVT, PE, renal vein thrombosis.
• Prophylactic anticoagulation: Not routinely required for all. Consider in high-risk patients after balancing risks.
• If confirmed thrombosis, treat with therapeutic anticoagulation.

[b]Infection Prevention:[/b]
• Assess promptly for fever/infection.
• Review vaccination status (pneumococcal, influenza, COVID-19).
• Avoid live vaccines in significant immunosuppression.
• [b]Important:[/b] Fever and abdominal pain in a patient with ascites require urgent assessment for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.

• Severe peripheral edema and anasarca.
• Pleural effusion and pulmonary edema.
• Acute kidney injury.
• Venous thromboembolism (Renal vein thrombosis).
• Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis and other infections.
• Hyperlipidemia and increased cardiovascular risk.
• Protein-calorie malnutrition.
• Vitamin D deficiency and metabolic bone disease.
• Hypothyroidism due to urinary loss of thyroid-binding proteins.
• Progression to chronic kidney disease (CKD) or kidney failure.

[b]Monitor:[/b]
• BP, daily weight (during active edema), edema and volume status.
• Urine output, serum creatinine, eGFR.
• Potassium, sodium, serum albumin.
• UPCR/UACR, lipid profile.
• Medication adverse effects.

[b]Outpatient:[/b] Hemodynamically stable, no significant AKI, edema controlled with oral therapy, no suspected thrombosis/infection.

[b]Hospital Admission:[/b] Severe generalized edema, AKI, severe hypoalbuminemia with complications, refractory edema requiring IV treatment, suspected/confirmed thrombosis, serious infection, significant electrolyte disturbances.

[b]ICU / HDU:[/b] PE with hemodynamic instability, severe pulmonary edema, shock, severe sepsis.

• Nephrotic syndrome is defined by heavy proteinuria (≥3.5 g/day in adults).
• Always quantify proteinuria using UPCR, UACR, or 24-h urine protein.
• Increases the risk of venous thrombosis and serious infections.
• Edema does not necessarily mean the patient has adequate intravascular volume.
• Use diuretics cautiously and monitor renal function and electrolytes.
• ACE inhibitors and ARBs reduce proteinuria but require monitoring of creatinine and potassium.
• Not every adult with nephrotic syndrome should receive empirical corticosteroids.
• Kidney biopsy is often important for determining the underlying pathology.
• Always investigate secondary causes (diabetes, lupus, infections, medications, malignancy).

• KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Glomerular Diseases, 2021.
• KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Evaluation and Management of Chronic Kidney Disease.
• KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Nephrotic Syndrome in Children.
• National Kidney Foundation (NKF). Nephrotic Syndrome.
• UpToDate. Overview of the Management of Nephrotic Syndrome in Adults.

[b]Clinical note:[/b] Adult nephrotic syndrome requires evaluation of the underlying histological diagnosis. Treatment should be individualized with nephrology input.

Tetanus:
[b]Emergency Medicine & Critical Care[/b]
Life-threatening neurological disease caused by tetanospasmin, a neurotoxin produced by Clostridium tetani.

Tetanus is caused by tetanospasmin, a potent neurotoxin produced by [b]Clostridium tetani[/b] (anaerobic, spore-forming bacterium).

• The toxin blocks inhibitory neurotransmission (GABA and glycine).
• Results in muscle rigidity, painful spasms, and autonomic dysfunction.
• [b]Important:[/b] Tetanus is not transmitted from person to person. Natural infection does not produce reliable immunity.

[b]Typical features:[/b]
• Trismus (lockjaw) - inability to open the mouth.
• Neck stiffness, dysphagia, difficulty swallowing.
• Generalized muscle rigidity.
• Painful muscle spasms triggered by light, sound, or touch.
• Risus sardonicus (facial grimacing).
• Opisthotonus (severe arching of the back).
• Abdominal muscle rigidity.

[b]Severe disease:[/b]
• Recurrent generalized spasms.
• Laryngospasm and respiratory muscle involvement.
• Autonomic instability (tachycardia, hypertension alternating with hypotension, sweating, fever, arrhythmias).

[b]Incubation period:[/b] Usually 3–21 days. Shorter incubation = more severe disease.

Tetanus is primarily a [b]clinical diagnosis[/b] based on characteristic symptoms and history of a wound or incomplete vaccination.

[b]Important:[/b]
• A visible wound may be absent or already healed.
• A negative wound culture does NOT exclude tetanus.
• Do not delay treatment while waiting for laboratory confirmation.

[b]1. Generalized tetanus:[/b] Most common. Rigidity, painful spasms, trismus. May progress to respiratory failure.

[b]2. Localized tetanus:[/b] Persistent rigidity/spasms near the injury site. May progress to generalized.

[b]3. Cephalic tetanus:[/b] Associated with head injuries/infections. Cranial nerve dysfunction, facial weakness, trismus.

[b]4. Neonatal tetanus:[/b] Infants of inadequately immunized mothers. Umbilical stump contamination. Inability to suck, irritability, rigidity, spasms.

[b]Immediate actions:[/b]
• Assess ABCs.
• Place patient in a quiet, low-stimulation environment.
• Minimize handling, light, and noise.
• Assess spasms, swallowing, and aspiration risk.
• Identify wound/source. Check immunization history.
• Arrange early ICU admission for severe disease.

[b]Red Flags:[/b]
• Severe/recurrent spasms.
• Apnea or respiratory distress, laryngospasm.
• Dysphagia with inability to handle secretions.
• Autonomic instability (severe HTN, arrhythmias).
• Rapidly progressive rigidity.

Diagnosis is clinical. Investigations assess complications.

[b]Labs:[/b] CBC, electrolytes (K, Ca, Mg), renal/liver function, glucose, CK (rhabdomyolysis), blood gas, urinalysis.

[b]Additional:[/b] ECG/cardiac monitoring, CXR (if aspiration), blood cultures, wound culture.

[b]Differential diagnosis:[/b]
• Strychnine poisoning.
• Acute dystonic reactions.
• Hypocalcemic tetany.
• Meningitis/encephalitis.
• Rabies.
• Neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
• Stiff-person syndrome.

Tetanus is a medical emergency requiring prolonged multidisciplinary care.

[b]Main goals:[/b]
1. Neutralize unbound toxin.
2. Stop further toxin production.
3. Control muscle spasms.
4. Maintain airway and ventilation.
5. Manage autonomic dysfunction.
6. Provide supportive critical care.
7. Complete active immunization.

[b]Purpose:[/b] Neutralizes circulating toxin not yet bound to nerve tissue.

[b]Dose:[/b] 500 IU IM once (CDC guidance). Some protocols use higher doses (follow local guidance).

[b]Administration:[/b]
• Give ASAP.
• If feasible, infiltrate part around the wound and give remainder IM at a separate site.
• Do NOT mix with tetanus vaccine in the same syringe/site.

[b]Important warnings:[/b]
• TIG cannot neutralize toxin already bound to nerve endings.
• Do not delay TIG for wound culture.
• Use human TIG over equine antitoxin when available.

• Identify the source of infection.
• Clean the wound thoroughly.
• Remove foreign material.
• Surgical debridement of necrotic/devitalized tissue when indicated.
• [b]Do not delay TIG or antibiotics while arranging debridement.[/b]

[b]Important:[/b] A wound may appear minor but still be associated with tetanus.

[b]Preferred: Metronidazole[/b]
• Dose: 500 mg IV every 6–8 hours.
• Duration: 7–10 days.
• Oral therapy if stable and able to swallow.

[b]Alternative: Penicillin G[/b] (per local protocols).

[b]Important:[/b]
• Antibiotics reduce further toxin production.
• They do NOT neutralize toxin already produced.
• Debridement remains essential.

[b]First-line: Benzodiazepines[/b] (enhance GABA inhibition).

[b]Diazepam:[/b]
• Initial: 5–10 mg IV slowly.
• Repeat/titrate per spasm control and respiratory status.
• Severe cases may need continuous infusion in ICU.

[b]Midazolam:[/b]
• Intermittent IV doses or continuous infusion in severe disease.

[b]Warning:[/b] Benzodiazepines cause respiratory depression and hypotension. Continuous infusions require close monitoring and airway support capability. Avoid unnecessary stimulation.

• [b]Magnesium sulfate:[/b] May reduce spasms and autonomic instability.
• [b]Neuromuscular blocking agents:[/b] Required in ventilated patients with severe refractory spasms.
• [b]Critical Warning:[/b] Neuromuscular blockade does NOT provide sedation or analgesia. Adequate sedation and analgesia must be maintained.

Autonomic instability may cause severe BP and HR fluctuations.

[b]Management:[/b]
• Continuous ECG and BP monitoring.
• Correct hypoxia, pain, fever, and electrolyte abnormalities.
• Magnesium sulfate (under ICU supervision).
• Short-acting agents (e.g., esmolol) for severe tachycardia/HTN.
• Treat hypotension with fluids and vasopressors when indicated.

[b]Warning:[/b]
• Avoid long-acting antihypertensives (BP is highly labile).
• Avoid excessive beta-blockade (risk of profound bradycardia and cardiovascular collapse).

[b]Indications for early airway intervention:[/b]
• Recurrent severe generalized spasms.
• Laryngospasm, respiratory muscle involvement.
• Apnea or hypoventilation, inability to protect airway.
• Severe dysphagia and aspiration risk.
• Requirement for deep sedation or neuromuscular blockade.

[b]Management:[/b]
• Early ICU and anesthetic assessment.
• Prepare for difficult airway.
• Endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation when indicated.
• Consider tracheostomy for prolonged support.

[b]Important:[/b] Do NOT wait for respiratory arrest before securing the airway.

• Quiet, low-stimulation environment.
• Adequate hydration and nutrition (enteral feeding when safe).
• Monitor fluid balance and urine output.
• Prevent pressure injuries.
• VTE prophylaxis when appropriate.
• Monitor for aspiration/VAP.
• Monitor CK, renal function, and urine output (rhabdomyolysis).
• Correct electrolytes.
• Adequate analgesia and sedation.
• Initiate rehabilitation/physiotherapy when appropriate.

[b]Important: Having tetanus does not provide reliable immunity.[/b]

• All patients recovering from tetanus should receive an age-appropriate tetanus-containing vaccine series.
• Use Td or Tdap according to age and national guidance.
• Do NOT administer the vaccine in the same syringe/site as TIG.

[b]1. Clean, minor wounds:[/b]
• Clean wound.
• Give vaccine if history incomplete/unknown, or last dose ≥10 years ago.
• TIG is NOT indicated.

[b]2. Dirty or major wounds:[/b] (Puncture, soil/feces/saliva, burns, crush, compound fracture, necrotic tissue).
• Give vaccine if history unknown/incomplete, <3 doses, or last dose ≥5 years ago.
• Give [b]TIG 250 IU IM[/b] if history unknown/incomplete or <3 previous doses.
• TIG is also indicated for HIV/severe immunodeficiency with contaminated wounds.

[b]Important:[/b] Antibiotics are NOT recommended solely to prevent tetanus after a wound.

• Respiratory failure.
• Laryngospasm.
• Aspiration pneumonia.
• Autonomic instability and arrhythmias.
• Rhabdomyolysis.
• Acute kidney injury.
• DVT and pulmonary embolism.
• Pressure injuries.
• Hospital-acquired infections.
• Prolonged muscle weakness and functional impairment.

[b]ICU Admission:[/b] Generalized tetanus, severe/recurrent spasms, respiratory compromise, autonomic instability, need for deep sedation/ventilation.

[b]Hospital Admission:[/b] Localized tetanus, suspected tetanus requiring specialist assessment, wound complications requiring surgery.

[b]Follow-up:[/b] Complete vaccination series, assess functional recovery, wound care, rehabilitation.

• Tetanus is a clinical diagnosis; treatment must not wait for labs.
• Trismus and painful spasms following a wound = immediate suspicion.
• TIG neutralizes ONLY unbound toxin.
• Wound debridement and metronidazole stop further toxin production.
• Benzodiazepines are central to spasm control.
• Severe tetanus may require prolonged mechanical ventilation and ICU care.
• Minimize light, noise, and unnecessary stimulation.
• Natural infection does not confer reliable immunity; vaccination is required.
• Always assess the airway early (laryngospasm and respiratory failure can be fatal).
